newsitem.title: USA: Ohio lawmakers slow school funding plan debate.
newsitem.headline: Ohio lawmakers slow school funding plan debate.

text.p: Ohio lawmakers debating public school financing reforms do not anticipate committee votes this week, an aide to the Senate president said Wednesday.

Legislative leaders had planned to advance school finance reform legislation through Senate and House committees this week in an effort to meet an August 6 deadline to approve necessary ballot referendums.
"In trying to work with the House, it is not going as quickly as we thought," said John Rabenold, an aide to Republican Senate President Richard Finan.

While no votes are anticipated this week from House committees, a substitute tax proposal for funding the reforms may be introduced Thursday, said Cheryl Burchard, spokeswoman for Republican House Speaker Jo Ann Davidson.

"We will likely have a substitute resolution tommorrow and will make some changes, but on the whole it will be the governor's plan," said Jack Hershey, administrative assistant to House Finance Committee Chairman Tom Johnson.
Ohio Supreme Court justices in March overturned the state's mostly property tax-based school funding formula and gave lawmakers one year to overhaul the system.

A task force appointed by Gov. George Voinovich has recommended increasing state aid by $1.1 billion in the current biennium and providing $5.8 billion for capital improvements over the next 10 years.
Task force members recommended increasing the state sales tax, the cigarette tax and property taxes on businesses and commercial properties to finance the program.
Senate Finance has begun reviewing tax increase proposals and fiscal accountability issues, including recommendations that school districts adopt "rainy day" funds and five-year budget forecasting.
House Education Committee members seek to add academic accountability to the package, while House Finance reviews the wording of the ballot questions.
Republicans hold a 21-12 majority in the Senate and would need no assistance from Democrats to reach the 60 percent margin needed to place a referendum on the November ballot.
While Republicans also hold a 60-39 majority in the House, legislative observers believe they need some support from Democrats to approve legislation.
Brian Rothenberg, spokesman for Ohio Senate Democrats, said minority senators recommend eliminating the inventory tax and substituting others for school funding.
Senate Democrats proposed making a 3.5 percent sales tax applicable to certain service providers, including lawyers and accountants, earlier this week.
School funding proposals have changed almost daily since lawmakers began reviewing the task force recommendations two weeks ago.
One plan would scale back funding reforms by increasing property tax relief, while approving proposed cigarette and sales tax hikes.

But all task force recommendations remained under consideration at mid-week, with the exception of a proposed referendum asking voters to choose who will decide appropriate education funding levels in the future, Rabenold and others said.
